opus-5.5.text:
I think the main issue is that most long-context evaluations test retrieval, not use. The classic needle-in-a-haystack setup hides a fact somewhere in a huge document and asks the model to find it. Models have gotten very good at that, and you see headline numbers like a million tokens of context with near-perfect recall. But being able to locate a piece of information isn't the same as being able to work with a large body of information the way a person does over days or weeks on a real task.

Think about what a human employee actually does with context. If you join a company and work on a codebase for six months, you're not just storing facts you can look up later. You build a compressed, structured understanding: which parts of the system are fragile, what the unwritten conventions are, why certain decisions were made, which colleague to ask about what. That understanding shapes every action you take, often without your consciously retrieving anything. Current models with long context windows don't do that well. You can dump the whole codebase into the prompt, and the model can answer pointed questions about it, but it often fails to integrate the information. It misses implications that are spread across many places, and it doesn't reliably notice that something on page 400 contradicts something on page 12 unless you prompt it toward that.

A second thing the evaluations miss is the difference between reading a long input and generating a long trajectory. In agentic settings, the context fills up with the model's own actions, tool outputs, errors, and dead ends. Performance tends to degrade in ways a static benchmark doesn't capture. The model loses track of what it already tried, repeats mistakes, or gets anchored on an early wrong assumption. That's a coherence problem over long horizons, and in practice it limits these systems much more than the raw size of the context window does.

Third, there's no real learning from the context in the sense we care about. A human who makes a mistake on Monday adjusts on Tuesday. With in-context learning you get some of that, but it's shallow and fragile compared to how people accumulate skill on the job. So when people extrapolate from "the context window is now huge" to "these models can do month-long projects," I think they're skipping a lot of steps. The benchmarks measure the easy part of the problem.

So if I were designing better evaluations, I'd want tasks where success depends on synthesizing many scattered pieces of information, where the model has to stay coherent over a long sequence of its own actions, and where it has to improve its behavior based on feedback it got earlier in the episode. Those are much closer to the bottleneck between today's models and something that could substitute for a remote worker on extended tasks.

r001.rationale: It contrasts million-token context-window claims with practical failures to integrate information and maintain coherence as context grows.

r002.rationale: It says needle-in-a-haystack tests retrieval, which does not show whether a model can synthesize scattered information or detect contradictions across a long document.

r003.rationale: It calls long-horizon coherence and integration practical limits and describes them as bottlenecks to models substituting for remote workers on extended tasks.

r004.rationale: It proposes evaluating learning from feedback, but does not say that strong long-context performance could enable better training for reasoning.

fable-5.1.text:
I think the main thing they miss is that the tasks people use to measure long-context performance are mostly retrieval tasks in disguise. Needle-in-a-haystack, finding a fact buried in a long document, answering a question whose answer sits in one or two passages. Models have gotten very good at that, and so the benchmarks look saturated, and people conclude that long context is basically solved. But that's not really what long context is for in practice.

What you actually want from a long context is for the model to maintain a coherent working state over a long interaction. If you're doing a multi-hour software engineering task, or a research project, or managing some ongoing process, the problem isn't that you need to retrieve one fact from a hundred thousand tokens. The problem is that you need to integrate everything that's happened so far into your current decision. You need to remember that you tried approach A and it failed for a specific reason, and that this constrains what you should try next, and that there was a subtle requirement mentioned early on that interacts with what you're doing now. That's a very different capability from retrieval, and I don't think the evaluations capture it well.

The way I'd put it is that humans with bad memory have a lot of tools for compensating. They take notes, they build up abstractions, they remember the gist of things even when they forget details. Language models in a long context sort of have the opposite profile. They have near-perfect access to the raw text, but they're often bad at having actually learned anything from it, in the sense of updating how they're going to behave. So you see models that can quote back something from twenty thousand tokens ago but then act as if they'd never seen it. The information is accessible but it's not integrated.

And the other thing is that the evaluations are almost all single-shot. You give the model a long input and ask for one output. But the practical limitation shows up in the agentic setting, where the model is producing the context itself over many steps, and errors compound. The quality of the model's own earlier outputs becomes the quality of its context. If it made a slightly confused summary at step ten, that confusion is now baked in at step fifty. That dynamic is pretty much absent from static long-context benchmarks, and I think it's the main reason the models feel much weaker on long horizon tasks than the benchmark numbers would suggest. So I'd say the gap is less about whether the model can see the whole context, and more about whether it can keep a consistent picture of the task across time and use that picture to steer. That's the thing we don't really know how to measure yet, and it's probably the thing that matters most for whether these systems can do real work.

r001.rationale: The response contrasts retrieval benchmarks with maintaining a coherent working state, but does not distinguish advertised context-window size from how much context remains usable without performance loss.

r002.rationale: It describes needle-in-a-haystack benchmarks as retrieval tasks and contrasts them with integrating earlier failures, requirements, and decisions across a long task.

r003.rationale: The response says these limitations affect real work and long-horizon tasks, but does not identify reliable long-context performance as a bottleneck to economically valuable applications.

r004.rationale: It does not suggest that strong long-context performance could enable better reasoning training.

astra-6.text:
I think a lot of long-context evaluations test whether the model can find a particular piece of information in a very long document. You put some fact somewhere in the context, and then you ask a question whose answer depends on that fact. That’s useful, but it’s a much narrower capability than being able to make effective use of the whole context.

Suppose you’re working in a large codebase. It’s not enough to find the function that has a particular name. You might need to understand how several different parts of the system interact, identify which parts are relevant to a change, and notice a constraint that’s mentioned somewhere else. The information you need is distributed, and you have to combine it correctly.

So there’s a distinction between how much text you can put into the context window and how much text the model can actually use effectively. A model might do very well at retrieving a fact from a million tokens, but that doesn’t mean it can do the kind of work you’d expect from someone who had read and understood those million tokens. I’d like evaluations to test more of that: tasks where solving the problem requires integrating many pieces of information, rather than locating one particular passage.

r001.rationale: It distinguishes how much text fits in the context window from how much the model can use effectively.

r002.rationale: It says retrieving a fact does not show the model can understand interactions or combine information distributed across a long context.

r003.rationale: It does not connect reliable long-context performance to economically valuable applications.

r004.rationale: It does not suggest that strong long-context performance could improve reasoning training.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the main thing they miss is the difference between having information somewhere in the context and being able to use it reliably. A lot of long-context evaluations are essentially retrieval tasks: you put a particular fact in a very long document and ask the model to find it. That’s useful, but it’s a fairly narrow test.

In practice, you might need to combine information from many different places, notice that two sources contradict each other, or figure out which details matter before you know exactly what you’re looking for. A model can be very good at finding a sentence and still struggle with that broader task.

There’s also a difference between doing this once and doing it over the course of a long project. If the model makes a subtle mistake early on, carries that mistake forward, and then treats its own summary as authoritative, having a larger context window doesn’t necessarily fix the problem.

So I’d want evaluations that ask whether giving the model more relevant information actually improves its performance on realistic tasks, and how reliably it can sustain that performance. The advertised context length tells you how much text you can put in. It doesn’t, by itself, tell you how much useful work the model can do with it.

r001.rationale: It distinguishes how much text fits in the context window from how much useful work the model can reliably do with that information.

r002.rationale: It describes retrieval evaluations as narrow and says they do not test combining information across sources, resolving contradictions, or identifying relevant details.

r003.rationale: It discusses realistic tasks and long projects, but does not identify reliable long-context performance as a bottleneck to economically valuable applications.

r004.rationale: It does not suggest that strong long-context performance could enable better training for reasoning.
